title: Thank them directly
hookLine: a gratitude letter read aloud gave one of the biggest short-term lifts in early studies

cards: Somewhere in your past is a person who changed your life and was never properly thanked. A teacher who saw something in you. A neighbor who drove you to the hospital.
A coach, an aunt, a friend who stayed on the phone until 3am. It's easy to tell other people about someone like that. Telling them is another matter.
For two days the thanks stayed inside you, on a list. Today it goes somewhere.

teach.b: In the same 2005 study that tested three good things, Martin Seligman's team tried another exercise, the gratitude visit. You write a letter to someone who was especially kind to you but was never properly thanked.
Then you deliver it in person and, if you can, read it aloud to them.
Of all the exercises in that study, this one gave the biggest boost in happiness in the short run, a clear jump right after the visit.
The lift held for about a month, then faded: a single gratitude visit is a big wave, not a new tide. A later study, by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, found something else.
Asked to predict how the person would feel getting their letter, the writers guessed too low. They expected it to be awkward, or not to matter much.
The people receiving the letters were more pleased, and less awkward, than the writers predicted. The researchers suggest this misjudgment may keep people from saying thanks at all.
So the research adds a push to do it on purpose, in words, with some detail.

teach.h: WHAT THEY DID, AND WHAT IT CHANGED.
teach.b: Not thanks for everything: what exactly they did, and what difference it made. Detail is what makes a thank-you land. And it doesn't have to be a long letter.
Three honest lines, said to them, count.

how: The gratitude visit, writing a letter to someone never properly thanked and reading it to them, is used in positive psychology courses and therapy, following Seligman and colleagues' 2005 study.

practice: Let one person come to mind, someone you've never properly thanked, and picture their face. In your head, shape three lines: what they did, what it changed for you, and what you want them to know now. Keep each one simple and true.

wordCard.voice: Epley. The researcher who found people guess too low about how much a thank-you letter will mean, a push to say it anyway. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: say it to them. Detail over drama: what they did, what it changed. That's day one hundred nineteen.
